Right now

Still learning, on purpose.

I'm in the OMSCS program at Georgia Tech focused on Human-Computer Interaction, and what pulled me toward it wasn't the interface design side — it was the psychology. Once you understand how people actually think and how technology changes their behavior, you start building systems and products differently: around the principles that make people actually want to use something, not just tolerate it. That's the edge I like working on — where business, technology, and psychology meet — and it's the same thinking I bring to the integration work every day.

Building has always been the hobby that turns into something bigger. That's what led me into Halo Studios' orbit and into building custom modes and mini-games inside Halo Infinite's Forge — and it's the same instinct behind the side projects: websites for local businesses, automations nobody asked for, and pushing AI tools past their obvious use cases just to see where they break. Some of it ships. Some of it's just for me.

Case Study

AI-Powered Campus Concierge Kiosk — turning a web AI agent into a public campus experience

College of Coastal Georgia · Electron · Node.js · Element451 · AI Agent Integration · Public Kiosk UX

01 · Role & Context

I designed and built the desktop kiosk application around Salty, CCGA’s existing Element451 AI concierge. The goal was not to create another chatbot. It was to take an AI service that already existed on the web and make it useful in a physical campus setting where a visitor can walk up, ask a question, and immediately open the resource connected to the answer.

I owned the kiosk application itself: the Electron shell, session behavior, split-screen experience, browser controls, link routing, privacy controls, idle handling, and the way the existing AI agent and College web resources work together inside one interface.

02 · The Problem

A normal website works well when someone is already on their own phone or computer. A public kiosk has different constraints. The person using it may not know the campus, may be standing in the building they are asking about, and should not have to understand which office owns a question before getting help.

There was also a UX problem with sending links from a chatbot. Opening a map, office page, or campus resource in the same browser can pull the user away from the conversation that got them there. On a shared device, there is a second problem: browsing state and chat state cannot be allowed to linger for the next person.

03 · What I Built

  • Split-screen experience: Salty stays visible on the left while campus maps, office pages, and other approved web resources open on the right.
  • Desktop kiosk shell: built the application in Electron and Node.js so the experience can run as a dedicated desktop app instead of relying on a user-managed browser window.
  • Link routing: external links and new-window behavior are intercepted and routed into the resource pane so the conversation remains in place.
  • Session controls: added Start Session and End Session flows, an inactivity warning, and automatic reset after the configured idle window.
  • Privacy-first browser state: each public-use session runs in a non-persistent partition, with local browsing and chat state cleared when the session ends.
  • Public-device hardening: downloads are blocked and permissions are denied by default, reducing what a walk-up user can leave behind or access from the kiosk.
  • Campus navigation support: the kiosk is designed around Salty’s campus-location knowledge and CCGA’s interactive campus map rather than treating directions as a separate experience.

04 · The Experience

The start screen makes the shared-device model explicit: begin a temporary session, use Salty and campus resources, then end the session and reset the local state for the next visitor.

Once a session starts, the AI and the campus resource remain side by side. In the example below, Salty stays open while the College’s interactive campus map is available in the second pane, with navigation and End Session controls remaining accessible at the top.

05 · Why Electron

The interesting part of this project was not simply putting two websites next to each other. The public-device requirements needed control over browser sessions, window behavior, external links, navigation, permissions, and reset behavior. Electron gave me a desktop application layer around the existing web services without requiring the College to rebuild Salty or the campus site.

That also kept the architecture deliberately simple: the AI remains in Element451, College resources remain on the web, and the kiosk owns the experience that connects them.

06 · Privacy & Session Design

A shared kiosk changes what “working” means. It is not enough for the page to load. The next visitor should not inherit the previous visitor’s browsing history, local storage, or conversation state. I designed session reset as a core behavior rather than an administrative cleanup step.

The application uses a non-persistent session partition for public use, clears local state when the session ends, blocks downloads, and denies permissions by default. Manual End Session and idle timeout both feed the same reset path so privacy does not depend on the visitor remembering to clean up after themselves.

07 · Current State

The working application now demonstrates the full kiosk flow: branded session start, embedded Salty experience, side-by-side campus resources, controlled navigation, end-session behavior, and automatic session handling. The next phase is the physical rollout work — kiosk hardware, Windows packaging and auto-launch, approved-domain controls, and final validation in the location where visitors will actually use it.

08 · What I’d Carry Forward

  • AI implementation is usually a systems problem. The model already existed. The value came from designing the experience, controls, and surrounding application that made it useful in a new context.
  • Shared devices need a different definition of UX. Session reset, permissions, and state isolation are user-experience requirements, not just security settings.
  • Keep the AI where it already works. Wrapping the existing Element451 agent avoided duplicating knowledge, analytics, routing, and maintenance in a second system.

Case Study

Salty — an AI support agent built around knowledge, routing, and human handoff

College of Coastal Georgia · Element451 Bolt AI · Conversational AI · Knowledge Base Architecture · Human-in-the-Loop Support

01 · Role & Context

I designed, built, and continue to operate the AI support experience behind Salty, the College of Coastal Georgia's virtual support agent in Element451 Bolt. My work covered the full support architecture around the model: knowledge design, conversational behavior, routing, verification, guided application-start workflows, escalation, human handoff, testing, and ongoing improvement.

The goal was not to replace staff. It was to make routine information available immediately, extend support beyond office hours, and make sure conversations that require a person reach the right team with enough context to continue.

02 · Production Impact After One Year

117,585

Human minutes saved · about 1,960 hours

7,856

Conversations handled by the agent

3,976

After-hours conversations · 50.6% of total

117

Human handoffs · just 1.5% of conversations

31,469

Knowledge Hub article references in the first year

226 / 252

Available knowledge sources referenced at least once · 89.7%

Normal staffed hours are 8:00 AM–5:00 PM, Monday through Friday. More than half of the agent's conversations occurred outside that window, giving students, prospective students, faculty, staff, and other users a support path when offices were closed. Across all 7,856 conversations, only 117 were transferred to a human — either because the request required additional support the agent was not designed to provide or because the user directly asked to speak with someone.

03 · The Problem

Institutional support is fragmented by design. Admissions, registration, financial aid, Help Desk support, housing, billing, orientation, Student Handbook guidance, and other services each own different answers and different processes. Users do not necessarily know which office owns their question, and many questions arrive after the office that can answer them has closed.

A useful AI support layer therefore had to do more than generate an answer. It needed to know what information it could safely provide, what required verification or access to an individual record, when to stop, and where to send the conversation next.

04 · What I Built

  • Knowledge architecture: built and maintain the institutional Knowledge Hub behind the agent. During the first-year reporting window, Element451 recorded 31,469 article references across 226 of 252 available knowledge sources, spanning admissions, academics, financial aid, housing, IT, student services, policies, and general College information.
  • Intent and routing logic: designed conversation paths that distinguish general informational questions from requests that need a specific office, workflow, or human response.
  • Human handoffs: configured escalation paths so conversations the agent should not resolve alone — or users who explicitly ask for a person — can be transferred to the appropriate service area. Only 117 of 7,856 first-year conversations (1.5%) used a human handoff.
  • Verification workflows: designed identity-verification paths for situations where the next step involves information tied to an individual student or applicant.
  • Guided application start: built a conversational path that helps prospective students begin an application to the College of Coastal Georgia, reducing friction between an information request and the next enrollment step.
  • After-hours support: structured the experience so users can still get useful assistance when College offices are closed instead of waiting for the next business day.
  • Testing and QA: review incorrect responses, failed escalations, routing issues, and knowledge gaps, then adjust the configuration and source material based on production behavior.
  • Training and documentation: created guidance and support materials so staff understand how the system works, where it hands off, and how the experience should be maintained.

05 · The Knowledge Layer in Production

The Knowledge Hub data gave me a better way to look at the agent than conversation volume alone. Across the same one-year window as the production metrics above, Element451 recorded 31,469 Knowledge Hub article references. Of 252 available sources, 226 were referenced at least once — 89.7% of the corpus.

That matters because it shows the support experience is drawing from a broad institutional knowledge set rather than leaning on a handful of FAQ pages. The heavily used sources also make the maintenance work more concrete: admissions requirements, technology help, financial aid, housing, student checklists, the Student Handbook, and other high-traffic content deserve closer review because small errors there can affect a large number of conversations.

The unused tail matters too. Twenty-six sources recorded no references during the period. Some are intentionally seasonal or niche, but that creates a useful audit list for stale content, duplicates, or sources that may no longer belong in the active knowledge set.

06 · Human-in-the-Loop Design

The most important design decision was treating escalation as part of the product, not as failure. A student asking for a general deadline may only need a grounded answer. A student asking about their own application, account, hold, bill, or other record-specific issue may need identity verification and a staff member with access to the underlying system.

I built those boundaries into the support flow so automation handles what it is good at while staff retain control of requests that require institutional judgment, protected information, or direct record access.

07 · Why the Metrics Matter

The strongest signal was not simply conversation volume. It was how much support the agent could deliver without requiring a transfer, and when that support was being used. Of 7,856 conversations in the first year, only 117 were handed to human staff — about 1.5% — while 3,976 occurred after normal business hours, approximately 50.6% of all usage.

I do not treat a handoff as a failure: some requests require staff access or judgment, and some users simply prefer a person. But the fact that only 117 conversations needed or requested that path shows how much of the College's routine support demand the agent was able to absorb. Combined with 117,585 human minutes saved — roughly 1,960 hours — the result is a support layer that extends service beyond business hours while reserving staff time for the cases where human involvement adds the most value.

Case Study

Post-Admit Checklist Modernization

College of Coastal Georgia · Element451 · Admissions, Housing, Registrar, Financial Aid, Bursar, Advising, Health Center, Academic Support & Technology Services

01 · Overview

After a student gets admitted, there's a gap between "you're in" and the first day of classes — orientation, housing, financial aid, immunizations, advising — and at most colleges that gap is held together by static PDFs, spreadsheets, and a lot of manual follow-up. This project moved that post-admit experience into a dynamic, trackable checklist inside Element451, so admitted students could see exactly what they still needed to do, and staff across departments could see exactly where things stood without chasing it down themselves.

02 · The Problem

Post-admit requirements were scattered across departments and mostly static — a checklist that looked the same for every admitted student regardless of their actual situation. That meant items that didn't apply to a given student still showed up, items that did apply weren't always visible at the right time, and "complete" usually meant someone on staff had manually checked a record and updated something by hand. Multiplied across every admitted student and every department involved, that's a lot of manual tracking, and a lot of room for a student to miss something simply because the system never told them it applied to them.

03 · My Role

  • Helped build and configure post-admit checklist items in Element451.
  • Created checklist logic tied to application and decision data.
  • Used condition-based checklist items so requirements only appeared when relevant to a given student.
  • Supported custom fields that stored checklist completion status behind the scenes.
  • Helped connect external system data to Element451 through imports and SFTP processes.
  • Worked across Admissions, Technology Services, Housing, Registrar, Financial Aid, Bursar, Advising, the Health Center, and Academic Support to get requirements right for each department.
  • Helped reduce manual tracking by letting checklist items complete themselves through rules, student input, custom fields, and imported data — instead of someone updating a record by hand.

04 · What I Built / Helped Implement

The core of this was a checklist experience that actually adapts to the student looking at it. Checklist items live in Element451's Decisions module, and each one can be active or inactive, required or optional, scoped to post-admit, and condition-based — meaning it only shows up if the student's data says it should. Behind that, custom fields track completion status quietly in the background, supplemental forms let a student's own input trigger an item's visibility or mark it complete, and SFTP/import processes feed in data from other systems to update those same fields. Put together, a student logs in and sees a checklist that reflects their actual situation, and staff get a record that updates itself instead of one they have to maintain by hand.

05 · Technical Approach

A few things had to work together correctly for this to hold up:

  • Checklist items in the Decisions module configured as active/inactive, required/optional, post-admit, and condition-based, so the same checklist template could behave differently per student.
  • Custom fields used as the source of truth for completion status, separate from whatever triggered that status.
  • Supplemental forms wired up so a student's submission could both capture their input and flip the checklist item's visibility or completion state.
  • SFTP/import processes that update records using student identifiers and status fields — Element451 matches the incoming data to the correct student, updates the relevant custom field, and the checklist logic marks the item complete based on how it's configured.

None of these pieces are exotic on their own — the work was in getting the conditions, fields, and data sources to agree with each other consistently across a few thousand student records and several departments' worth of requirements.

06 · Results

This is still early — the dynamic post-admit checklist went live for Fall 2026 admitted-student processes, so what follows are early indicators from that first term, not an audited, long-term institutional result. With that caveat:

  • Early indicators show stronger admitted-student engagement with post-admit requirements overall.
  • Orientation registration increased by an estimated 18%.
  • Housing applications increased by an estimated 22%.
  • Completion of required post-admit information before the first day of classes improved by an estimated 26–30%.

As the process runs across more terms, I'd expect completion rates, student clarity, and staff visibility to keep improving — this is the first data point, not the ceiling.

07 · What I Learned

Most of the hard part wasn't Element451 configuration — it was getting Admissions, Housing, Registrar, Financial Aid, Bursar, Advising, the Health Center, and Academic Support to agree on what "required" and "complete" actually mean for their piece of the checklist, and translating that into conditions and fields that don't contradict each other. That's a cross-department coordination problem before it's a technical one, and it's part of why I've gotten more interested in the human side of these systems — not just whether something is technically configured correctly, but whether the person looking at it on the other end actually understands what it's asking them to do.

Case Study

AI-Driven Admissions Scoring System

College of Coastal Georgia · Element451 Bolt Agent Platform · Nursing, Radiology & Honors Programs

01 · Overview

Nursing, Radiology, and the Honors Program each run competitive, requirement-heavy application cycles — the kind where every applicant needs to be checked against a specific set of prerequisites before a program can make a decision. I built the full workflow for all three: checklist logic to track requirements, an AI-driven analysis layer on Element451's Bolt Agent platform that scores each completed application against program-specific requirements, and a post-acceptance layer that gives admitted students the information they need to be ready for day one in their program.

02 · The Problem

Nursing and Radiology in particular have hard requirements — specific prerequisite courses, minimum grades, documentation — that someone previously had to check by hand, application by application, after the window closed. That review process alone was adding roughly two extra months on top of the application period before either department had a finalized applicant pool to make decisions from. Admitted students also often didn't get clear, upfront information about what they needed to do to be ready for their first day, since that guidance depended on the same manual process finishing first. Honors faced a related but different problem: a manual, less structured review process that made it harder to move quickly on decisions as application volume grew.

03 · My Role

  • Designed checklist logic to track application requirements per program (Nursing, Radiology, Honors).
  • Built an AI-driven analysis layer on Element451's Bolt Agent platform that evaluates each completed application against program-specific requirements.
  • Configured scoring output as not qualified, qualified, or highly qualified, giving staff a fast, consistent first-pass read before manual review.
  • Built the post-acceptance information flow so admitted Nursing and Radiology students receive the requirements and preparation details they need ahead of their first day.
  • Worked with each department to define what their specific requirements actually meant in checklist and scoring logic.

04 · What I Built

The core of the system is a scoring layer that reads a completed application against a program's defined requirements and returns a consistent first-pass rating — not qualified, qualified, or highly qualified. Staff make the final decision on every application; the score gives them a fast, consistent starting point instead of a cold read on every file. That alone removed most of the manual requirement-checking that had been adding months to the process. Layered on top of that, I built out post-acceptance guidance specifically for Nursing and Radiology, so once a student is admitted they immediately get the program-specific requirements and preparation information they need to be ready for day one, rather than finding out piecemeal. The one fully automated exception is the Windward Scholar pathway — dual-enrollment students continuing to CCGA after high school — where the decision itself is automated based on their existing dual-enrollment record.

05 · Results

These are department-reported outcomes, not independently audited figures:

  • Nursing and Radiology went from roughly two extra months of manual post-window review to about a week to finalize their applicant pool.
  • Both departments reported being able to make admissions decisions noticeably faster as a direct result.
  • Admitted Nursing and Radiology students now receive clear, upfront requirements and preparation information instead of learning what they need piecemeal after acceptance — helping them arrive better prepared for day one.
  • The Honors Program saw an increase in applications received, alongside an easier, faster application and decision process for staff.

06 · What I Learned

The time savings here came less from "AI scoring" as a novelty and more from removing a specific, well-defined bottleneck: manual requirement checking that had to happen serially, application by application, before anything else could move. Once that first-pass read became consistent and fast, everything downstream — decisions, post-acceptance communication, staff bandwidth — moved faster too. It also reinforced that keeping human review in the loop wasn't a limitation on the automation; it's what made departments comfortable trusting a faster process in the first place.

Case Study

Service Workflow Automation System

Marshline AI · AWS Serverless · Amazon Connect · Built for service-based small businesses (plumbing & HVAC)

01 · Overview

This is a reusable workflow automation system I built for service-based small businesses — plumbing and HVAC-style companies, specifically — that replaces manual phone-and-paper intake with a structured, automated request pipeline. It's not a chatbot bolted onto a website. It's a full intake-to-ticket workflow built on AWS serverless architecture, with an optional AI-assisted intake path layered on top for after-hours calls or when nobody's at the desk to answer.

02 · The Problem

Small service businesses run on phone calls and whoever happens to be at the desk to take them. When that person isn't available — after hours, mid-job, out for the day — requests either don't get captured cleanly or get captured with half the details missing, which means someone has to call the customer back just to fill in the gaps. That doesn't scale, and it doesn't leave a clean, technician-ready record of what was actually requested.

03 · My Role

  • Designed and built the serverless backend using AWS S3, Lambda, and API Gateway.
  • Designed the structured intake schema — name, contact info, address, service type, issue description, urgency, and preferred follow-up method.
  • Built the email routing so a completed, technician-ready request lands directly with the business.
  • Designed the AI-assisted intake workflow concept using Amazon Connect for after-hours and hands-off scenarios.
  • Worked directly with a real business — Karate's Plumbing — to validate the workflow against how their office actually operates day to day.

04 · What I Built

At its core, the system gives customers or office staff a way to submit a service request online instead of relying entirely on a phone call — capturing the same structured information every time: name, contact info, address, service type, issue description, urgency, and how the customer wants to be followed up with. That submission runs through a backend AWS workflow and comes out the other side as a completed request emailed straight to the business, formatted so a technician can pick it up and go without having to track anyone down for missing details. It's built to be adapted across multiple service-based businesses with similar intake needs — the same backend pattern, with the fields and routing tuned per business.

05 · Technical Approach

  • AWS S3 hosts the intake interface and static assets.
  • API Gateway is the entry point for every submission, regardless of how it came in.
  • AWS Lambda handles backend processing — validating and structuring the submitted data.
  • Email routing fires automatically once a request is processed, with no manual step in between.
  • The intake schema and routing logic are kept separate from the backend itself, so the same architecture can be reused for a different service business without a rebuild.

06 · AI-Assisted Intake

The system also includes an AI-assisted intake path built on Amazon Connect — not as a separate product, but as another door into the same backend. A customer calls in, answers a defined set of questions, and those responses get turned into the same structured service-request format as a web submission, then sent through the same pipeline to reach the business. The point isn't "add a chatbot" — it's giving the system a way to capture a clean request even when nobody's available to answer the phone.

07 · Business Impact

These are estimates based on early business feedback and observed workflow improvement, not audited metrics:

  • Reduced manual intake and ticket-creation effort by an estimated 30–40%.
  • Reduced customer callback needs by an estimated 25–35%.
  • Saved roughly 3–5 administrative hours per week for a small service office.
  • Improved after-hours request capture by an estimated 20–30%.
  • Reduced incomplete service-request details by an estimated 25%.

For Karate's Plumbing specifically, the practical feedback was simpler than any of those numbers: the office secretary didn't have to be physically present to handle intake anymore. She could answer calls remotely and submit the ticket herself, plumbers picked up requests with clearer information already attached, and the business lost less time calling customers back just to collect details that should've been captured the first time — especially on after-hours requests.

08 · What I Learned

The useful insight here was separating "how a request comes in" from "what a request needs to contain." Once those are decoupled, a phone call, a web form, and an AI-assisted intake call can all feed the exact same backend without the business ever seeing a difference in what lands in their inbox. It also reinforced something I keep running into at a much larger scale in my day job: the simplest automation that a small office will actually use beats a more sophisticated one that doesn't fit how they actually work.

Case Study

Policy Navigator — an internal AI assistant for institutional policy

College of Coastal Georgia · Internal tool for staff and faculty · Microsoft 365 Copilot Agent Builder · SharePoint · Python · SQLite

01 · Role & Context

I designed, built, and did the source architecture for Policy Navigator — an internal tool for staff and faculty at the College of Coastal Georgia, built on Microsoft 365 Copilot Agent Builder, SharePoint, and Python.

02 · The Problem

The College publishes roughly eighty policies covering everything from annual leave to procurement thresholds to acceptable use of technology. All of it is available. Almost none of it is findable.

Staff generally know a rule exists without knowing which document contains it, which office owns it, or whether the version they remember is still current. The predictable result is that questions with published answers land in the inboxes of HR and Business Affairs, and the people best positioned to handle judgment calls spend their time on lookups instead.

The gap wasn't publication. It was retrieval.

03 · What I Built

A grounded question-answering assistant that reads the College's own policy corpus and returns a direct answer, the source document it came from, and the office responsible for it.

The design constraint that shaped everything: in a policy context, a confident wrong answer costs more than no answer. A tool that is helpful 90% of the time and quietly invents the other 10% is worse than useless — it's a liability, because users can't tell the difference.

Three decisions followed from that:

  • Grounding is enforced at the platform level, not by instruction. The agent is configured to answer only from attached sources. Asking a model nicely to avoid general knowledge is not a control; restricting what it can retrieve is.
  • Every answer carries provenance. Policy title, section, and revision date where the source shows them — never inferred. Users can verify and escalate rather than take the tool's word for it.
  • Absent information is named, not filled. The assistant is explicitly instructed to state what it doesn't have and stop, rather than reaching for something plausible.

04 · The Interesting Problem: Scoping

College policy sits underneath system-level policy from the University System of Georgia — three manuals, one of which is 230 separate documents behind a platform with no automated export.

Including it fully would have delayed launch by weeks for material that is secondary to most questions. Excluding it created a subtler risk: College policies cite system policy constantly, so the assistant would encounter those references inside documents it did have. The danger wasn't a gap in coverage. It was that a language model, seeing a familiar-sounding requirement, would fill the gap convincingly from general knowledge.

I scoped to College policy only and handled the seam explicitly. When a source cites a system requirement, the assistant names the reference exactly as written and describes nothing about it, directing the user to the responsible office. The boundary is stated in the assistant's operating instructions, reinforced in its prohibited behaviors, and disclosed in the closing line of every substantive answer.

I also scoped and prioritized a 35-document subset of the system manual covering the domains staff actually ask about — purchasing, travel, compensation, accounts payable — so the decision is reversible once usage data shows whether it's needed.

05 · Source Engineering

Most of the work was not in the assistant. It was in the corpus.

The policy repository served content as a single dynamic page containing every policy at once — fine for humans, poor for retrieval, since finding one paragraph inside one enormous document is a much harder problem than picking the right document from eighty. I wrote a Python tool to split the corpus into one file per policy, preserving title, responsible office, and effective and revision dates as structured headers, and producing an inventory of the full set.

That inventory turned out to matter more than the split. Sorting by revision date surfaced a set of documents that hadn't been touched in over a decade, several containing unfinished drafting — placeholder text, truncated definitions, empty required sections — and a number of internal links pointing at a retired content management system.

An AI assistant surfaces that material faithfully and at volume, where a rarely-visited repository does not. I routed the findings to the policy owners before launch and added an instruction requiring the assistant to flag incomplete source text rather than repeat it as policy.

A second tool maps cross-references between policies and reports which cited documents are missing from the knowledge base, so the corpus can be closed iteratively rather than guessed at.

06 · USG Policy Crawler & Publishing Layer

USG policy created a different problem. A large portion of the system-level material lives in PolicyStat pages that are public to read but aren't packaged in a way that works well as a controlled AI knowledge source. Rather than rely on Copilot to interpret that site directly, I built a Python crawler and publishing pipeline around it.

The crawler starts with discovery, collects approved policy links and stable PolicyStat IDs, then fetches each policy and extracts the parts that actually matter: policy number, title, status, effective and revision dates, owner, policy area, sections, body text, and source references. I preserve the raw HTML as well, then write normalized policy records to JSON and smaller JSONL chunks that can be used for search or AI ingestion.

SQLite keeps crawl state and history, and each run produces a report showing what was discovered, attempted, succeeded, or failed. The first full HR pass discovered 83 policies, which gave me a real set to validate the parser and metadata handling against instead of testing on a couple of hand-picked pages.

The last step is a static publishing layer. Each normalized USG policy becomes its own clean HTML page on a CCGA-controlled site, with navigation and search. That gives the AI a much simpler retrieval target and also gives us a way to test every layer independently: USG source → crawler → normalized data → published HTML → Copilot retrieval.

The next iteration is an incremental sync instead of a full recrawl: compare stable policy IDs, revision metadata, and content hashes; fetch only new or changed policies; preserve version history; and flag removed or changed content for review before publishing. That turns the crawler from a one-time scraper into a maintainable policy synchronization service.

07 · Outcome

Pilot in progress — to be updated with usage volume, question categories, and accuracy against the known-answer test set.

Evaluation is a fixed set of questions with verified answers, drawn from the domains that generate real traffic rather than edge cases. Failures drive instruction revisions. The set gets rerun after each change, which means "did that fix it" is a measurable question rather than an impression.

08 · What I'd Carry Forward

  • The corpus is the product. Model capability was never the limiting factor. Document structure, freshness, and coverage were — and that's where the effort belonged.
  • Scope down to ship. The comprehensive version of this tool was achievable and would not have launched. A narrower one that works, with a documented path to expand, was the better trade.
  • Design the failure mode first. Deciding what the assistant does when it doesn't know shaped the instructions more than any decision about what it does when it does.
  • Tools like this need an owner, not just a builder. Documents change, and an assistant grounded in a stale corpus degrades silently. Naming who maintains it was part of the handoff, not an afterthought.

Flagship case study · Marshline AI

AI Evaluation & Quality Platform

Marshline AI · 2026 · Completed independent demo · React · GitHub Pages

01 · Overview & My Role

I designed and built the AI Evaluation & Quality Platform as an independent Marshline AI project. The completed browser-based demo brings test-suite management, AI system and version tracking, evaluation runs, quality dashboards, and reporting into one workflow.

The goal is to make a release decision traceable: what was tested, which rules were applied, what failed, and what needs attention before a version moves forward. This is independent work, separate from CCGA’s employer-owned systems.

02 · Why I Built It

I wanted to go beyond building AI assistants and work on the question that follows: how do you know they are working well enough to trust? A convincing answer in a demo is only a starting point. I built this project to explore repeatable testing, regression detection, and the operational decisions that sit between an AI prototype and a responsible release.

03 · The Problem

Changes to prompts, sources, or system configuration can improve one behavior while breaking another. An overall quality score can hide missing citations, a policy violation, or a failure to hand a sensitive question to a person. Teams need a consistent test set and explicit acceptance criteria so they can explain why a version is ready, needs review, or should be blocked.

04 · Deterministic Evaluation & Scoring

The evaluation engine uses deterministic, explainable rules for checks that need repeatable outcomes. Given the same response, test expectations, and rule configuration, scoring produces the same result. Individual check results support the overall score so a reviewer can see the reason for a failure.

  • Response quality: compare outputs with the test case’s explicit requirements and expected behavior.
  • Citations and groundedness: check required citation evidence against defined source expectations. Rule-based checks do not establish that every natural-language claim is factually correct.
  • Policy compliance: evaluate defined policy requirements and prohibited behavior.
  • Escalation: test whether cases that require a human handoff receive the expected escalation behavior.

This keeps objective controls auditable. A future production version could add an LLM-based judge for subjective qualities such as clarity or semantic relevance, with calibration and human review; it would complement the deterministic checks.

05 · Regression Testing & Failure Analysis

Version comparisons expose changes in individual quality dimensions alongside the aggregate score. Rerunning a consistent suite makes it possible to spot newly failing cases and distinguish an improvement from a tradeoff.

Illustrative synthetic example: a candidate version could increase overall quality from 89% to 94% while citation quality falls from 96% to 90%. The citation regression still needs attention even though the headline score improved. These numbers illustrate the comparison; they are not measured production results.

Failure analysis connects a failed case to its evaluation checks so the next action is specific: revise response guidance, improve source coverage, adjust escalation behavior, or correct a test expectation. The suite can then be rerun to check the fix and look for new regressions.

06 · Release Gates & Governance

Release gates translate evaluation results into three explicit outcomes: Ready for Release, Needs Review, or Blocked. The status reflects transparent criteria rather than an aggregate score alone. A critical policy or escalation failure can block a release even when its overall quality score is high.

Governance checks bring release requirements into the same review as model behavior. They make missing requirements visible before someone treats a passing score as permission to deploy. The demo supports an explainable readiness decision; organizational approval, access enforcement, and deployment control belong in a production workflow.

07 · Latency, Cost & Reports

Latency and cost sit alongside quality so version comparisons can reveal operational tradeoffs. A response that meets its quality requirements still has to fit the service’s response-time and spending expectations.

Quality dashboards and exportable evaluation reports make runs, version comparisons, failures, and release status easier to review and share. The purpose is to give both technical and business stakeholders a clear account of what passed, what changed, and what needs attention.

Latency and cost values in the synthetic demo illustrate the reporting workflow; they are not live provider benchmarks or verified operating costs.

08 · Public Demo Architecture

The React application is hosted as a static site on GitHub Pages. Evaluation runs in the browser, with local browser storage supporting the demonstration workflow. No paid API or application backend is required to explore it.

GitHub Pages → React application → browser evaluation engine → deterministic checks → scoring, regression comparison, and release gates → local storage and exportable reports.

This architecture makes the completed project easy to demonstrate and inspect. Local browser storage is a convenience for a demo; it is not a shared evaluation database or a tamper-resistant audit log.

09 · Synthetic Data Disclosure

The public demo uses synthetic demonstration data to show test cases, AI responses, evaluation results, and version comparisons. It does not present real student, employee, or client records, and its example scores are not evidence of production accuracy, organizational adoption, or business impact.

The demonstrated outcome is a completed evaluation workflow: define tests, evaluate behavior, compare versions, inspect failures, review release readiness, and export the findings.

10 · Production Architecture Considerations

A production deployment would extend the static demo with services and controls appropriate to the organization. These are proposed production requirements, not claims about the current GitHub Pages application.

  • Secure application API: authentication, role-based access, tenant boundaries, and server-side secrets for model integrations.
  • Persistent evaluation records: a shared database for versioned suites, rule configurations, response evidence, run history, and review decisions, with retention and access policies.
  • Execution pipeline: queued evaluation jobs, provider adapters, retry handling, rate limits, and reproducible run metadata.
  • Release integration: automated regression runs in CI/CD, enforced release gates, named approvers, and an audit trail for exceptions.
  • Monitoring: measured provider latency, token usage and cost, failure rates, and changes in response quality over time.
  • Data governance: redaction of sensitive data, approved test datasets, encryption, and controlled report access.

11 · What This Demonstrates

This project connects AI implementation to quality and operations. I translated the broad question “can we trust this version?” into testable requirements, explainable checks, version comparisons, and a review workflow. It reflects how I approach solutions engineering: understand the business decision, build the system around it, and make the result understandable to the people responsible for using it.
